studies.title: With Reason And A Term
studies.meaning: Two claims sit side by side before any argument begins. The scripture comes down from God, named here by power and wisdom together. Then creation is said to have been made with truth and for a set term, which denies two things at once: that the universe is purposeless, and that it is permanent. The closing clause does not argue with those who refuse. It reports their posture. They are turning away from a warning already delivered, which makes the difficulty attention rather than evidence.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the later stretch of the mission there, when opposition had hardened from curiosity into settled refusal. The surah opens the way its six immediate predecessors open, and shares their concerns: where the Book comes from, the emptiness of what is worshipped alongside God, and the ruin of earlier peoples. No specific occasion is reported for these opening ayat. The commentators read them as the surah stating its own subject before it begins.

keyTerms.note: A verbal noun, not a verb, so the phrase names the act rather than narrating it. The form carries a sense of gradual descent, which suits a book delivered across two decades.
Literally a named limit. The second word means it has been specified, not merely that one exists, which makes the end of the world a fixed appointment rather than an eventual wearing out.
From a root meaning to present one's side. The image is a body angled away rather than a mind that has weighed and rejected, so refusal is described as a bodily habit.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything the first listeners owned had a term on it. A lease on a well ran out. A truce between tribes held for a named number of years. Dates were bought before harvest against a stated date, and a debt fell due on a day both parties could count to. Arabic had a precise vocabulary for such deadlines. Saying that the heavens and the earth carry one placed the sky in a category they already knew how to think about.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the last of seven consecutive surahs, numbers forty to forty-six, that open with the same two disconnected letters. All seven were revealed in Mecca, and the tradition of reciters has long treated them as a family. The group is the longest unbroken run of surahs in the Quran sharing an identical opening.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage joins revelation and cosmology in one breath, and the join is the argument. A universe made with purpose and given a deadline is a universe in which a warning makes sense; a universe that simply is would make any message beside the point. The two divine names chosen carry the same pairing. Power without wisdom would be arbitrary, and wisdom without power could not act on what it saw.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle in the surah immediately before this one, and adds that each soul is repaid.
Denies that the heavens and the earth were made in play, using the negative form this passage uses.
Puts the appointed term inside a call to reflect on oneself, rather than in an argument with opponents.

studies.applyIt: Pick one object near you that you expect to outlast you, a building or a hill on the horizon. Give it a number of years. You will be wrong, and that is the point of the exercise. The passage says the sky itself has a date on it. Holding that thought for thirty seconds tends to rearrange what feels urgent.

studies.title: Show Me What They Made
studies.meaning: The challenge is framed as a request for evidence, and it names the two kinds that would count. Either produce something in the world these objects have made, a patch of earth or a share in the heavens, or produce a text: an earlier scripture, or any surviving trace of transmitted knowledge. The demand is not that opponents feel differently. It is that they show their working. The last clause makes truthfulness the standard, so the argument is about honesty as much as about proof.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The shrine at the centre of the city held images associated with a long inherited practice, and its authority came from age and custom rather than from any book. The surah presses exactly there. Its opening ayat had claimed a scripture sent down from God; this one asks the other side for the equivalent. No particular occasion is reported. The commentators treat it as part of the surah's opening argument about origins.

keyTerms.note: From a root for a track left behind. It covers a fragment of transmitted learning handed down from earlier generations, so the challenge accepts oral tradition as evidence and still asks for it.
The ordinary commercial word for a stake in a venture. Used of the heavens it makes the claim measurable: name the portion these objects own, the way a partner names his.
A command to make visible, not to explain. It asks for something that can be pointed at, which is a harder demand than the argument the opponents were prepared to have.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca ran on evidence of a particular kind. A trader's reputation rested on witnesses who had seen a transaction. Genealogists carried lineages in memory and could be challenged on a name. Poets were judged in public, line against line, before crowds who knew the older verses. A city that assessed claims this way could recognise the shape of this request even when it did not like where it pointed.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase rendered as a trace of knowledge occurs only here in the whole Quran, and its exact reading was discussed early: some reciters read the word as a single trace, others with a form suggesting selection or a chosen report. All the readings keep the sense of something inherited from earlier generations rather than freshly reasoned.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts the burden of proof on inherited practice rather than on the new message, which reverses the usual direction of religious argument. It also sets out what would count against a claim, in the world or in a text, and by doing so treats belief as something answerable to evidence. Truthfulness appears at the end as a moral quality bound to an intellectual one: saying what you cannot show is placed among the failures of character.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same double demand almost word for word: what have they created, and where is their book.
Asks opponents for a clear authority and tells them to bring their scripture if they are truthful.
Applies the same standard to any claimant: produce your proof, whoever you are.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you hold firmly and ask yourself where you first got it. Not whether it is right, only where it came from. Most convictions turn out to have arrived from somebody rather than from evidence, and noticing that is not the same as abandoning them. It is the habit this ayah is asking for, turned on yourself first.

studies.title: A Call That Never Arrives
studies.meaning: The failure described is not that the call is refused. It is that nothing at the other end is listening. Two separate defects are named: no answer will come, and the ones addressed are unaware that anyone is addressing them. The time limit given is not a short one. The silence runs to the Day of Resurrection, so no future moment will correct it. Then the scene shifts to that day, when the objects of all that devotion become opponents and disown the worship they were given.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage follows a demand for evidence and moves from argument to consequence, which is the surah's habit. Pilgrimage to the Meccan shrine was a fixed part of the regional year, and appeals were made there for rain, for safe caravans, for children. No specific occasion is reported. The commentators read the passage against that ordinary practice rather than against any single incident.

keyTerms.note: A form that means to answer a request, not merely to reply. The word is used elsewhere of God answering prayer, so its denial here is precisely targeted at what the caller wanted.

Heedlessness rather than refusal. It describes something that never registered at all, which is a colder verdict than rejection: the prayers were not heard and then declined, but simply never arrived.
The plural of a word used for open hostility between tribes. On that day the relationship inverts completely, and what was petitioned for help stands on the other side of the case.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A petition in that world went through a patron. A man without a strong clan sought protection from a chief, and the arrangement was public: the protector announced it, and everyone knew whose name stood behind whom. Its value depended entirely on the patron acknowledging you when the moment came. The nightmare was arriving at a crisis and finding that the man whose name you had been using did not know who you were.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses the same verb for calling on God and for calling on anything else, and the difference is carried by what follows, not by the word itself. In this passage the identical verb appears in one ayah for the act and its result. The neutrality of the verb is why the argument here has to be about the answer rather than the asking.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage measures worship by whether it lands, which is an unusual test. Sincerity is not questioned; the callers are assumed to mean it. What fails is the receiving end. That separates devotion from its object and refuses to let the intensity of feeling validate its direction. The scene of disowning on the last day extends the point: attachments formed in this life do not bind the thing attached to.

crossReferences.why: Says the same objects do not hear the call, and would not respond even if they did.
Gives the direct contrast: God is near and answers the call of the one who calls.
Shows the same reversal, where what was taken as support becomes a denier and an opponent.

studies.applyIt: Notice, once today, where you actually turn first when something goes wrong. Not what you would say if asked, but the reflex: a person, a screen, a plan, a name. The passage is not asking you to feel guilty about it. It is asking you to see the direction of the turn, because you cannot redirect a habit you have never watched.

studies.title: Clear Called Obvious Magic
studies.meaning: The sentence is built so that two words collide. The signs are recited plain and clear; the verdict returned is that this is obviously magic. The same adjective sits on both sides. Whatever quality made the recitation unmistakable is the quality being cited as proof of sorcery, which is the point: the effect was admitted and only its source was disputed. Note also what is not said. No counter-argument is offered, only a label, and the label conveniently ends the conversation.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. By this stage the recitation was being heard in the streets and at the shrine, and its effect on listeners was a practical problem for the city's leadership. Classical sources describe attempts to discourage visiting pilgrims from listening. Calling it sorcery was one of a set of charges, alongside poetry and soothsaying, that placed the words in a known category and so removed the obligation to weigh them.

keyTerms.note: A form meaning not merely clear but clarifying, something that makes other things plain. Applied to the recited signs it claims they carry their own evidence rather than needing external support.
In seventh-century usage it covered anything that produced an effect by hidden means, including persuasion so powerful it seemed uncanny. The charge concedes the power while relocating its cause.
The same root as the word used a moment earlier for the clarity of the signs. Placing it on the accusation makes the ayah's irony structural rather than a matter of tone.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia had recognised specialists in powerful speech. Soothsayers spoke in short rhymed bursts and were consulted about lost camels and disputed paternity. Poets were believed by many to draw on a companion spirit, and a satire from a famous one could damage a tribe's standing for a generation. A man who heard extraordinary words had ready categories for them, and reaching for one of those categories was the ordinary response, not a desperate one.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact phrase translated here as obvious magic appears nine times across the Quran, and in almost every case it is spoken by opponents about a revelation or a miracle, including by Pharaoh's court about Moses. The repetition is part of the argument: the same verdict is shown being returned in different centuries by different people.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates rejection after recognition rather than before it. What is described is not a failure to perceive but a decision about how to file what was perceived, which makes the moral weight fall on the naming rather than on the hearing. It also sets a limit on what evidence can accomplish. Clarity is granted by the ayah itself, and clarity turns out not to be sufficient, because a name can be found for anything.

crossReferences.why: Records the identical verdict, and adds that they returned it the moment truth reached them.
Shows Pharaoh's people saying the same words about the signs given to Moses.
Preserves the reasoning behind the charge: this is transmitted magic, this is human speech.

studies.applyIt: Catch yourself the next time you reach for a category before you have finished listening. The word might be naive, or political, or overrated. Notice that the label arrived faster than any thought, and let the sentence finish anyway. You can still reject it afterwards. The passage is about the gap between hearing and filing, and that gap is where attention lives.

studies.title: If I Had Invented It
studies.meaning: The reply does not begin by denying the charge. It takes the accusation and follows it forward: if the messenger had fabricated this, the accusers could do nothing to shield him from what would come of it. That is a strange defence, because it lets the charge stand while pointing out that those making it have no stake in the outcome. The dispute is then handed over. God knows what they are pouring themselves into, and He is enough as witness. The last words are forgiveness and mercy, which is not where a quarrel usually ends.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a stretch of the surah where objections are quoted and answered one at a time. Fabrication was the central charge in Mecca, and it was a serious one in their own terms: attaching invented speech to God was a grave act, not a clever tactic. No particular occasion is reported. The commentators read the ayah as one reply in a sequence the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was instructed to give.

keyTerms.note: From a root for cutting and shaping hide. Fabrication in Arabic is a made thing, cut to fit, which is the exact charge: that the words were tailored to a purpose rather than received.
A verb of overflowing, used of a flood leaving its banks and of a crowd streaming down from a plain. Applied to talk it pictures people carried along by their own conversation.
Courtroom vocabulary. A witness settled matters that argument could not reach, and naming God as the sufficient one moves the case to a court neither side in Mecca could convene.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca settled its quarrels by arbitration and by oath. When two parties could not agree, they went to a man both sides respected and accepted his judgement, or one of them swore a binding oath in the sanctuary and the matter closed. Both methods needed a third party everyone trusted. In a dispute over whether words had come from God, the city had no such arbiter available, and the ayah names one anyway.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for what the opponents are engaged in comes from a root meaning to overflow. The same verb appears where the Quran describes pilgrims streaming down from the plain of Arafat, and again where it describes a community caught up in passing along a rumour. It occurs in this particular form only twice in the whole Book.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes truthfulness the hinge of the whole claim, which is a risky place to put it. A fabricator would be exposed by God rather than refuted by opponents, so the messenger's safety is staked on his honesty and on nothing else. The two names at the end complicate the exchange further. Having described accusers who will not listen, the ayah closes with the door left open rather than shut.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same charge from the other direction, by inviting the accusers to produce a comparable chapter.
States what would follow if the messenger had attributed invented sayings to God.
Closes another dispute over the message by calling God a sufficient witness between the two sides.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next argument you find yourself inside where neither side can be checked by anything outside itself. Politics, family history, who said what. Watch how much of the heat comes from the absence of a referee. The ayah does not settle its dispute either. It relocates it, and then stops talking. You can do the same thing today, once.

studies.title: I Am Not Unprecedented
studies.meaning: Three denials in one sentence, and the middle one is the surprising part. The messenger is not a novelty; others came before on the same terms, so the office is old even where the man is new. Then he is made to say that he does not know what will be done with him or with them, which the commentators generally read as concerning outcomes in this life rather than final destiny. What remains is stated positively and it is very little: he follows what is revealed to him, and he warns plainly. Authority is redescribed as receipt.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Part of the Meccan objection was that no messenger had ever been sent to their city, so the claim looked like an invention without precedent. Alongside that ran a demand for the kind of knowledge a seer was expected to have, about buried treasure, about the future, about who would die. This ayah answers both at once. No specific occasion is reported for it in the classical sources.

keyTerms.note: From a root for originating something with no model behind it. It occurs once in the Quran, and the sentence carrying it is a denial: the messenger is refusing the description, not claiming it.
A passive form. The verb covers swift and hidden communication, and the passive removes the messenger from the sentence: he is where the words arrive, not where they begin.
A warner arrives before the danger, not after it. The word implies time still remaining, so the role carries a mercy inside it that the English noun does not obviously hold.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia had a figure for this. When a raiding party was sighted, a man ran ahead of it to the camp, and by custom he stripped as he ran so nobody could mistake his urgency for ordinary news. The proverb about him was old before Islam. He carried no plan and no remedy, only the information and the time it bought. Everyone hearing the word for warner had that running man somewhere in mind.
studies.didYouKnow: The word translated as unprecedented occurs exactly once in the whole Quran, here, and its root gives Arabic its ordinary term for an innovation. The one place the Book uses it, the word is being pushed away rather than claimed: the sentence exists in order to say that the speaker is not the first of anything.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a boundary around prophecy that the tradition has kept carefully. A prophet is a recipient, not a source, and his knowledge is not enlarged in general but only where he is told. That distinguishes the office from divination, which claims access on demand. It also lands hard on the human side: the man delivering the warning stands under the same uncertainty about tomorrow as the people receiving it.

crossReferences.why: Lists the same denials at greater length: no divine treasuries, no knowledge of the unseen, not an angel.
Adds what would follow if he did know the future, which is that he would have secured much good.
Tells him directly that nothing is being said to him that was not said to earlier messengers.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing about your own next year that you have quietly decided you know. A job, a relationship, a diagnosis, a move. Say the sentence of this ayah about it, in your own words, and stop there without adding a reassurance. Most people find the honesty easier to carry than the forecast was.

studies.title: A Witness Who Recognised It
studies.meaning: The argument runs as a hypothetical the listener is invited to hold for a moment without accepting it. Suppose it is from God and you have refused it. Beside that supposition a fact is placed: someone raised on an earlier scripture recognised the kind of thing this is and believed, while you grew large in your own eyes. The commentators differ over who the witness is, some reading a named contemporary, others Moses, others the class of learned Israelites. The verdict closes on arrogance rather than on argument.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Jewish and Christian communities lived across the peninsula, in Yemen, in Najran, in the oasis towns to the north, and Meccan traders dealt with them. Their scholars had a standing the Meccan leadership recognised, which is what makes the comparison bite. The classical sources discuss whether this ayah reflects a later moment, since the surah is otherwise Meccan, and they record that discussion without settling it.

keyTerms.note: Literally have you seen, used in Arabic as tell me, or what do you say to this. It opens a hypothetical without conceding it, inviting reasoning about a case the listener has not granted.
Not the book itself but something of its kind. The witness is described as recognising a type, which is what long study of an earlier scripture would make possible before any detailed comparison.

keyTerms.gloss: you grew large, you were arrogant
keyTerms.note: A form meaning to seek greatness for oneself. The Quran uses it for a posture rather than a conclusion, which is why it stands opposite believing here instead of opposite knowing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Expertise in that world was personal and portable. A man who had memorised a scripture carried it in his chest, and communities travelled to consult such people about law, lineage and the interpretation of dreams. Meccan caravans passing north through Syria met monks and rabbis whose learning they respected without sharing. When such a person accepted a claim, that carried weight in exactly the currency Mecca understood, which is why the comparison stings.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran opens an argument with this exact plural form, have you considered, twelve times, usually to set up a supposition the listener has not granted. The nearest twin of this ayah stands in the surah numbered five earlier, where the same opening leads to the same hypothetical: what if it really is from God, and you have rejected it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats refusal as a moral event rather than an intellectual one. Nobody in it is shown failing to understand; someone with the relevant training understands immediately. What separates the two responses is a stance toward being taught, which the ayah names as self-enlargement. The closing clause follows from that. Guidance is withheld not from the ignorant but from those whose posture has made receiving anything impossible.

crossReferences.why: Poses the identical supposition, and asks who could be further astray than someone who rejects it.
Describes those given knowledge before it falling on their faces when the recitation is read to them.
Shows recipients of an earlier scripture saying they had already submitted before this arrived.

studies.applyIt: Think of a subject where someone you consider less qualified than you turned out to be right. Sit with the memory for a minute without explaining it away. The ayah's charge is not ignorance but size, the way knowing a lot can make it hard to be told anything. Notice where you are currently too large to be corrected.

studies.title: They Would Have Got There First
studies.meaning: The objection quoted here is not about the message at all. It is about who accepted it. If this were worth anything, the argument runs, people like us would have reached it before people like them, so the low standing of the early believers is offered as evidence against the claim. Truth is assumed to arrive in order of rank. The second half predicts the next move: having refused to be guided by it, they will reach for a dismissal that costs nothing, calling the whole thing an old fabrication.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The first community was made up largely of the young, of women, of men without powerful clans, and of enslaved people, some of whom were tortured by their owners for it. Mecca's leadership found the composition of the group embarrassing before it found the message threatening. Classical sources describe requests that the poor be removed from the assembly before the notables would sit and listen.

keyTerms.note: The verb of racing, used of horses and runners reaching a mark first. It turns belief into a contest of precedence, and the objection assumes the order of the field was fixed before the race began.
From a root meaning to overturn. It names not a mere error but a truth stood on its head, which makes it a heavier accusation than calling something mistaken.
Old, and by implication worn out. Calling the falsehood ancient dismisses it twice over: it is untrue, and it is not even new, so no one need trouble to answer it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan society was legible at a glance. Where a man sat in an assembly, whose protection he carried, which clan buried his dead, all of it was public and none of it moved much in a lifetime. A person without a clan behind him could be beaten in the street with no consequence. In a city read that way, the social standing of a new group looked like a fact about the group's claims.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran puts almost the same objection in much older mouths. Noah's opponents dismiss his followers as the lowest among them at a glance, and elsewhere the comfortable ask whether these are really the ones God has favoured out of everybody. Reasoning from rank is presented as one of the standard responses to a prophet, not a Meccan invention.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage exposes a hidden premise rather than answering the objection. If truth travelled by status, then nothing could ever reach a society from below, and every established arrangement would be self-confirming. By quoting the argument instead of refuting it, the ayah lets its shape do the work. The second clause adds something colder: a verdict about the message follows the refusal rather than causing it.

crossReferences.why: Noah's notables use the identical reasoning, objecting that only the lowest among them have followed him.
Records the demand to drive away the poor believers, and the question about whom God has favoured.
Corrects the same instinct at its root, when a blind man is passed over for a man of standing.

studies.applyIt: Watch for the version of this you actually use. It rarely sounds like snobbery now. It sounds like noticing who is recommending something, and deciding in advance how seriously to take it. Pick one idea you have filed away because of who was carrying it, and give it fifteen honest minutes on its own terms today.

studies.title: Confirming, In An Arabic Tongue
studies.meaning: Two books are set in relation and the relation is described precisely. The earlier one is called something to take bearings from and a mercy, which are functions rather than praise. This one is called confirming, meaning it declares the earlier true rather than replacing it, and then it is located in a language. The last clause splits its audience in two without splitting the book: the same words warn those doing wrong and carry good news to those doing good. Which one you hear depends on where you are standing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Scripture in that region was mostly heard in languages the Arabs did not read. Communities in Yemen, Najran and the northern oases had Hebrew, Syriac and Greek texts, and Arabic had a great oral literature but no scripture of its own. Some Meccans used this against the new message, arguing that revelation belonged elsewhere. The ayah answers by naming the language as part of the claim rather than a limitation on it.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary word is for a person walked behind or a road taken. Applied to a book it means something you steer by, not merely a text you assent to or admire from a distance.
An active form built on the word for truth. It does more than agree with what came before: it stands as a witness for it, which makes the later book testify on the earlier one's behalf.
From a root for the skin, because news shows in the face before it reaches speech. The word is for tidings that visibly change a person, set here directly opposite a warning.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Language marked the edges of that world. A Meccan trader on the Syrian route heard liturgy in Greek and Syriac and understood none of it, and interpreters were a recognised trade at the frontier markets. Slaves in the city spoke Persian, Ethiopic and Aramaic. Poetry was the one thing Arabic did better than anyone, judged in public at seasonal fairs. A scripture in that language arrived inside the one form the audience was expert in.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause naming the Book of Moses here appears word for word in only one other place in the Quran, in the surah about Hud. The phrase used for the Arabic tongue, however, occurs nowhere else at all; elsewhere the Book calls itself an Arabic recitation, four times, and once describes itself as coming in a clear Arabic tongue.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes revelation cumulative rather than serial. A later book that confirms an earlier one is claiming continuity of source, which means the test of a new scripture includes its relation to what preceded it. Naming the language matters for the same reason. Revelation is described as arriving inside a particular tongue and a particular audience, not floating above them, which is what makes it possible to be warned by it at all.

crossReferences.why: Contains the same clause about the Book of Moses, a model and a mercy, in a different argument.
Traces the descent of the revelation onto the heart and names the clear Arabic tongue it arrived in.
Answers directly what would have been said had the recitation come in a language they did not know.

studies.applyIt: Read a page of translation today with the fact of translation in front of you. Notice one place where the English had to choose, where a word carried two things and only one survived. You are not being asked to learn Arabic this afternoon. You are being asked to hold, for one page, the awareness that something is being handed to you through a door.

studies.title: A Sentence And A Life
studies.meaning: After several ayat of quoted objections, the other side of the argument is defined, and the definition is short enough to be startling. A statement about who the Lord is, and then a course kept afterwards. Nothing appears about lineage, wealth, eloquence or success, which is pointed given the objection just quoted about social rank. The consequence arrives in the negative first, no fear ahead and no grief behind, and only then in the positive. The closing clause ties the outcome to what they were doing habitually, in a form that describes a practice rather than a moment.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, placed immediately after opponents dismiss the believers as the wrong sort of people. The community at that stage was small, largely without protection, and defined in the city's eyes by who its members were. A definition that mentions no rank at all answers that setting directly. The classical commentators report no particular occasion, and read the pair as the surah's positive counterweight to the objections it has been collecting.

keyTerms.note: A particle of sequence with a gap in it, unlike the connective meaning simply and. Placing it between the statement and the steadiness makes the second thing later and separate, not part of the same breath.
The word for the people you travel and camp with, and for the members of a trade. Calling them companions of the Garden makes belonging there a settled association rather than a visit.
From a root for lasting without ageing, used in Arabic of mountains and of things that do not wear out. It carries permanence more firmly than the English forever, which is often said loosely.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Security in that world was a matter of who your people were. A man belonged to a clan, and the clan answered for him; lose that and you were open to anything. Fear had a shape, and so did grief, because both were tied to a standing that could be withdrawn by an assembly of men. Promising a group with almost no standing that neither would reach them was a claim about a different kind of belonging.
studies.didYouKnow: The promise of no fear and no grief occurs eleven times in the Quran, and the description it attaches to changes each time: those who follow guidance, those who spend their wealth by night and day, those who believe and set things right, the friends of God. Here it attaches to the shortest description of all, a sentence and then a course held to.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are being held together that often come apart. The passage is unmistakably about a stance of the heart, since it begins with a statement, and unmistakably about conduct, since it ends with a reward measured against practice. Neither swallows the other. The order matters too. The declaration comes first and the steadiness follows it in time, which places the difficulty of religion after its beginning rather than at its threshold.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same two-part definition and describes angels descending on those who keep to it.
Attaches the identical promise to a different short definition: submitting the face and doing good.
Repeats the promise for the friends of God, and adds that His words do not change.

studies.applyIt: Take the sequence seriously for one day. The declaration you can make in a second; the holding is the part that costs. Choose something small you already know you drift from, a prayer time, a habit of speech, the hour you sleep. Do not improve it. Just keep it exactly as it stands, today, and notice what keeping costs.

studies.title: Thirty Months And A Prayer
studies.meaning: The instruction is brief; the reason takes over the sentence. The mother's labour is named twice with the same word, in pregnancy and in delivery, before any duty is spelled out. Then the ayah jumps forward to a man of forty and gives his words rather than his deeds: a prayer to be enabled to be grateful, to act well, and to have his own children set right. Gratitude to parents and to God are folded into one request.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a surah that alternates between argument with Meccan leaders and portraits of individual response. Reports attaching this ayah to a particular companion circulate in the commentaries, but they differ over who is meant and the classical writers generally read the wording as describing any believer who reaches middle age. The contrast is with the son in the ayat just after, who answers his parents with contempt.

keyTerms.note: The same word covers what is repugnant and what is carried against inclination. Repeating it for bearing and for delivering refuses to soften either, and it is stated as fact rather than as a claim on the child.

A rare imperative asking to be held to something, used elsewhere in the Quran only by Solomon. The man does not ask for gratitude to appear; he asks to be gathered and restrained until he produces it.
A plural-shaped noun for the peak of a person's powers, used of Joseph and of Moses at the point where each was given judgement. Here it is paired with an exact number of years, which is unusual.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Childbirth in seventh-century Arabia was survived rather than managed. Women delivered at home with the help of relatives and a midwife, and a family could name the babies it had lost as readily as the ones it kept. Nursing ran close to two years, and a mother's milk was a bond strong enough to create kinship in Arab custom. Thirty months was a measurable stretch of a woman's life, not a figure of speech.
studies.didYouKnow: Read beside two other passages, this one yields a piece of arithmetic the classical scholars noticed early: thirty months for carrying and weaning together, and two full years given elsewhere for weaning alone, leaves six months for the pregnancy. The deduction is one of the oldest examples of reading two separated ayat as a single statement.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Kindness to parents is grounded in something already done rather than in authority, so the claim is presented as a debt of fact. The prayer at forty then turns the whole ayah forward: the mature believer does not ask to repay his parents but to be made capable of gratitude, which means the capacity itself is treated as a gift. Repentance is placed at the end, in a life that has gone well.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same enjoinment with a different image, weakness upon weakness, and supplies the two years this passage assumes.
Turns to the moment the relation reverses, when a parent grows old and the child is asked for gentleness in speech.
Contains the only other use of the rare verb in this prayer, on Solomon's lips after he overhears an ant.

studies.applyIt: If a parent of yours is alive, ask them one factual question this week about the year you were born: where they lived, what the work was, what they were afraid of. Do not turn it into an apology or a thank-you. The ayah begins with information, not sentiment, and most people find they are missing more of it than they expected.

studies.title: The Best Of What They Did
studies.meaning: Two verbs describe an accounting that is deliberately uneven. On one side, the best of what a person did is taken up and received; on the other, the wrongs are stepped past. Commentators read the first phrase in more than one way, either that the finest deeds are singled out for acceptance, or that everything is accepted and the whole is rewarded at the rate of the best. Both readings agree on the asymmetry. Nothing here says the record is falsified. It says which end of it is used.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayah closes a short sequence that began with a definition of the believers and passed through a portrait of someone who honours his parents and turns to God at forty. The surah then moves immediately to its opposite. The commentators treat this as the summary of the first portrait rather than an independent statement, and report no specific occasion for it.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form of accepting, used of a gift welcomed rather than merely taken. The same verb appears where Abraham and Ishmael ask that the work of their hands be accepted from them.

keyTerms.gloss: We pass over, We go beyond
keyTerms.note: To walk past something and keep going. The picture is of moving beyond a thing rather than scrubbing it away, which is a different image from washing clean, and it occurs in this form only here.
Not simply a true promise. The construction attaches truthfulness to the promise as a quality it possesses, so what guarantees it is the character of the one promising rather than its wording.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Debt in Mecca was recorded and remembered. A man's obligations were known in the market, and creditors could hold a defaulter or his children against what was owed. Forgiving a debt was a public act, done in front of witnesses, and it cost the forgiver something real. The idea of an account settled by the creditor stepping past the worst entries would have sounded to that audience like an extraordinary piece of generosity rather than a technicality.
studies.didYouKnow: Both of the verbs in this ayah, the accepting and the passing over, appear in this exact first-person plural form only once in the whole Quran, here. The Book describes God overlooking wrongs in many places, but this particular pairing, in which the best of a life is taken up in the same breath as the worst is walked past, is not repeated.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage says something specific about how a life is weighed. A person is not summed up but read selectively, and the selection is generous rather than neutral. That undercuts two errors at once: the assumption that God's justice means an exact tally, and the assumption that mercy means the record does not matter. The record matters, and the reading of it is a mercy, and the two are stated in a single sentence.

crossReferences.why: States the same exchange plainly: misdeeds remitted, and reward given for the best of what they did.
Puts it the other way round, acquitting them of the worst and rewarding them by the best.
Describes smaller wrongs being remitted for those who keep clear of the gravest ones.

studies.applyIt: Do this for one person today rather than for yourself. Pick someone whose worst moment with you is easy to recall, and deliberately call up their best one instead, in the same detail. Notice how much harder the second is to reconstruct. That difficulty is the habit the ayah is describing, run in the opposite direction from the one you are used to.

studies.title: Generations Have Passed Before Me
studies.meaning: The objection has the shape of evidence. Generations went into the ground and none of them came back, so the promise of being raised is treated as refuted by the record. Underneath the argument sits contempt, delivered in a single syllable to the two people who raised him. The parents do not counter with reasoning. They call out for help and press one urgent word, and he answers with a label rather than a reply. The label he reaches for is the same one Mecca used against the recitation itself.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, placed directly opposite the portrait a few ayat earlier of a man at forty giving thanks for his parents. The commentators record a disagreement about whether a particular individual is meant, and most read the passage as a type rather than a biography, since the surah is holding two lives side by side. Denial of resurrection was the central Meccan objection, argued exactly this way, from the silence of the graves.

keyTerms.note: Not a word so much as a noise, the sound made at something soiled or wearisome. Arabic grammarians class it as standing in for a whole sentence of complaint that is never spelled out.
The verb used for shouting under attack or from deep water. Its form here describes action still going on, so the parents are pictured pleading continuously rather than speaking once.
A plural tied to lines of writing and to things set in rows. It suggests stories copied and handed on, so the charge is about transmission rather than about someone inventing them now.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Old age in that world had no institution behind it. A man who could no longer travel or trade depended entirely on his sons, and the arrangement was visible to everybody in a small city. Arabs also carried their ancestors with them, reciting lineages and taking pride in the graves of the dead. Both facts sit inside this scene: a son with all the power, and a family argument conducted over the ancestors' silence.
studies.didYouKnow: The syllable of exasperation here occurs three times in the Quran. Once it appears where the Book describes what a child owes ageing parents, naming this exact sound as the thing not said to them. Once Abraham throws it at the idols of his people. The third time is this ayah, where a son aims it at his mother and father.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates denial inside a family rather than in an assembly, which changes what is at stake. An argument about resurrection turns out to be inseparable from how a person treats the two people whose decline is the nearest evidence of mortality he has. It also shows the argument from absence in its purest form. Nothing has come back, therefore nothing will, which is a claim about the future built from a sample of the past.

crossReferences.why: Draws the opposite portrait a few ayat earlier, of a man at forty praying for himself and his parents.
Names this same syllable in describing what is owed to a parent grown old in one's care.
Gives the identical objection from earlier peoples, ending in the same dismissal as old tales.

studies.applyIt: Call whichever parent or elder is easiest to put off, and let the conversation run past the point where you usually end it. You are not solving anything. The ayah puts an argument about eternity inside a room with two ageing people in it, and the tone in that room turns out to be part of the argument. Notice yours.

studies.title: The Word Falls Due
studies.meaning: The verdict is described with the vocabulary of a debt rather than of a decision. The word became due upon them, the way a payment falls in on a fixed date, which puts the outcome at the end of a process instead of at the whim of a judge. They are then placed inside a long series of earlier communities, and the series is said to include jinn as well as humans, so the reckoning reaches beyond the visible world. The closing word is a merchant's term for the party who ends with less than he started.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just set two lives against each other, one turning to God in maturity and one dismissing his parents' faith, and this ayah delivers the second man's verdict. Jinn appear repeatedly in this surah, and a passage near its end describes a group of them listening to the recitation. No specific occasion is reported here; the commentators read it as the summary of the preceding portrait.

keyTerms.note: The verb behind the nouns for truth and for a right that is owed. Saying the word became due on them borrows the language of an obligation falling in, not of a sentence being pronounced.
A group held together by something shared rather than by blood; the Quran uses the same word of birds and animals. Its plural here strings jinn and humans into one continuous line.

keyTerms.gloss: those who end at a loss
keyTerms.note: A trader's word for the side of a transaction that closes with less than it opened. It measures a whole life the way a ledger measures one season of buying and selling.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca lived by seasonal accounting. Money was raised for a caravan, goods went north or south, and months later the venture closed at a profit or a loss that everybody in the city could name. Partnerships were dissolved, shares divided, and a man's standing rose or fell on the figure. Describing a person as one who came out at a loss placed his whole existence inside the only reckoning his neighbours took entirely seriously.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of jinn and humans occurs eight times in this exact form in the Quran, and this surah is one of the very few places where the jinn are given a scene of their own rather than a mention. A group of them is described near the end of the surah as arriving to listen, then hurrying back to warn their people.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two claims sit inside a short sentence. The first is that judgement is earned rather than imposed, since the language is that of something falling due. The second is that moral accountability is not a human peculiarity: another order of creature is described as living under the same terms and reaching the same outcomes. Together they make the reckoning look less like a courtroom built for people and more like a condition of being made at all.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase about a sentence becoming due, on communities of jinn and humans that passed before.
Gives the jinn their scene later in this surah, listening and then carrying the warning home.
Shows the successive communities arriving one after another, each disowning the one before it.

studies.applyIt: Take one running commitment of yours and work out its actual date. A course you meant to finish, a debt, a promise made in a good mood. Write the date down. The ayah's picture of a word falling due only works if you already know the feeling of a term arriving, and most of us keep that feeling deliberately vague.

studies.title: Degrees For Every One
studies.meaning: The word for degrees is plural and it is given to everyone, which quietly complicates the two-sided picture the surah has been building. Both outcomes are graded from inside; nobody is simply sorted. The verb that follows belongs to weights and measures, meaning to hand over the full amount agreed with nothing shaved off the top. Then the sentence ends on a denial rather than a promise. They will not be wronged is a smaller and more exact claim than saying they will be rewarded, and the smallness is the point.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the surah's comparison of two lives before it turns to the scene at the Fire. The commentators note that the word for everyone here covers both groups already described, not only the second, and they draw from it the idea of ranking within each destination. No specific occasion is reported. The surah's argument at this stage is about accountability, which was the point the Meccan opponents refused.

keyTerms.note: The steps of a stair or the tiers of a building. A plural rather than a pair, so the picture is a gradient with many positions rather than two rooms with a wall between them.
Built from the root for completing a measure. It is the merchant's word for handing over the exact quantity agreed, which is why the ayah adds no promise of anything above it.
To wrong is, at the root, to put a thing somewhere it does not belong. The denial is therefore about placement: no one is set at a level his own work did not reach.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Short measure was the standard fraud of that economy. Grain, dates and oil were sold by volume, and a merchant with a shaved measure or a weighted scale could take a little from every customer for years without being caught. Traders carried their own weights and checked them, and disputes over a measure could set two families against each other. The vocabulary of paying in full was heard in the market long before it was heard here.
studies.didYouKnow: This plural for degrees appears in only four places in the Quran in exactly this form. Two of them are near twins: this ayah and one in an earlier surah open with identical words and then close differently. In a third, a group is not said to have degrees at all but simply to be degrees in the sight of God.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Justice is defined here by subtraction rather than by generosity. A person receives exactly what his own work amounts to, and the guarantee offered is that nothing will be taken from him unfairly. That leaves reward and mercy to be spoken of elsewhere and keeps this sentence honest. It also implies that a life has a magnitude, not merely a verdict, which is why a gradient rather than a boundary is what the ayah describes.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle almost identically, degrees for each according to what they did.
Shows the same root raising ranks for those who believe and those given knowledge.
Gives the companion promise: whoever does good need fear neither injustice nor loss of his due.

studies.applyIt: Think about one thing you did this year that nobody noticed and nobody credited. Do not tell anyone about it now. Just register that it is on the record somewhere, at its exact size, neither inflated by an audience nor lost for want of one. That precision is what the ayah is offering, and it is worth more than praise.

studies.title: You Used Up Your Good Things
studies.meaning: The address is made at the moment of exposure, and its subject is consumption rather than belief. The charge is that the good things were spent in the earlier life and enjoyed there, with nothing held back. The commentators are careful here: the word used is the Quran's ordinary term for wholesome provision, so the pleasant things are not being condemned. What is described is a portion taken entirely in advance. The two reasons given at the end are arrogance without warrant and habitual transgression, so a posture and a practice, not an opinion.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The city's leading families had grown rich on the caravan trade and on their custody of the sanctuary, and their confidence in that comfort is a recurring subject in the Meccan surahs. The commentators connect this ayah to that setting rather than to a single incident. It follows immediately after the statement that everyone is graded by his own work, so it shows what one such grade looks like from inside.

keyTerms.note: The same word the Quran uses for permitted food and for good provision generally. Nothing in it implies excess, which is why the ayah has to specify where the things were spent rather than condemning them.
A causative form: not they were lost but you caused their going. It places the disappearance in the hands of the people addressed rather than assigning it to the passage of time.
From a root for lightness and low worth. The punishment is named by the shame inside it rather than by its pain, which answers directly the self-enlargement named later in the same sentence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Comfort in Mecca was imported and visible. Silk and brocade came up from Yemen, wine and worked leather from Syria, perfume along the incense road. A wealthy household ate meat regularly while poorer families did not, and hosted feasts that the whole quarter could see. Standing was displayed by what a man could afford to consume in public, which is exactly the register this ayah answers, and it answers it with the word for shame.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for a punishment of shame appears three times in the Quran, and its other two occurrences are attached to specific cases: those who invent a revelation and claim it came from God, and the people of Thamud, who are described as preferring blindness once guidance had reached them. Here it is attached to nothing more dramatic than a comfortable life spent entirely on itself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does not treat pleasure as guilt. It treats it as a drawing down, which is a different idea and a harder one. What a person enjoys is real and is his, and the question the ayah raises is only whether anything remains on the other side of the ledger. The reason clause keeps this from becoming a rule about comfort: arrogance and transgression are named as the actual charges, and the spending is their evidence.

crossReferences.why: Carries the same phrase about a punishment of shame, there for inventing a revelation.
Describes the arrogance of Aad in the same terms, and a punishment of shame in this life.
Sets out the whole logic behind this charge: rivalry in wealth and children, then a harvest that withers.

studies.applyIt: Look at one pleasant thing you will have today, a coffee, a hot shower, a meal somebody cooked. Do nothing about it except register that it came from somewhere and that you did not arrange it. The ayah is about a life spent without that registration, and the correction is not less enjoyment. It is noticing while you enjoy.

studies.title: Warned Among The Dunes
studies.meaning: The messenger is introduced by kinship rather than by office. He is their brother, one of them, which the commentators identify as Hud, sent to the people of Aad. His message is compressed to a single clause and a single fear expressed on their behalf. What is unusual is the parenthesis: warners had passed before him and would come after him, so his arrival is placed inside a sequence rather than presented as a unique event. The location is named, and it is the one place in the Quran that word occurs.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Aad were remembered in Arabian tradition as a powerful people of the deep south who were destroyed, and their ruin was proverbial long before this surah. Meccan trade ran along the incense route through country associated with them, so the audience knew the story as local history rather than as foreign legend. The classical commentators place the dunes in the sandy region toward the south of the peninsula without fixing a precise site.

keyTerms.note: Curved ridges of sand, the shape wind leaves behind. The word occurs once in the Quran and gives this surah its name, which makes a landscape feature the title of the whole chapter.
Kinship rather than rank. The Quran introduces several messengers to their own peoples this way, which frames each of them as an insider making a demand rather than a stranger arriving with one.
A plural that can carry either the men who warned or the warnings they brought. Read either way it sets this messenger inside a line running both before and after him.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The southern route was lined with evidence of collapse. Caravans out of Mecca passed abandoned irrigation works, dead wells and stone foundations in country that could no longer support the population it once had. Traders told stories about the people who had built them. Sand moves, and a dune that has swallowed a settlement is a slow and entirely visible thing, so a warning delivered among the dunes needed no explaining to that audience.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah is named after a word that occurs exactly once in the Quran, in this ayah. Several surahs take their names from rare words, but few from a term used only a single time. The word describes a specific landform rather than a doctrine or a person, which makes the title a place name for a chapter mostly concerned with argument.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage denies prophecy any claim to novelty at the very moment it recounts one. By noting warners before and after, it makes this messenger an instance of a pattern, which is the same point made earlier in the surah about the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). It also shows what a warning consists of when reduced to its core: one instruction about worship, and one fear held on someone else's behalf.

crossReferences.why: Tells the same episode at length, with Aad's reply and the outcome that followed it.
Gives another full account, including their appeal to the strength of their forefathers.
Recalls Aad in a short oath passage, asking what was done with the people of the columns.

studies.applyIt: Notice the difference between warning someone and lecturing them. This messenger states a fear he holds for the people in front of him and stops. If there is somebody whose direction worries you, try saying only that, once, in one sentence, without the argument attached. Then leave it alone for a week.

studies.title: Bring It, If You Are Truthful
studies.meaning: Two moves are made in one short reply. First the message is reframed as interference: he has come to turn them off their gods, which makes the whole thing an attempt on their loyalties rather than a claim about the world. Then they demand the threatened punishment immediately, which looks like an argument and is really a dare. If the warning were true, they reason, it would already have arrived. The verb they choose for turning them away is built on the same root as the word for a fabrication, so the accusation is that he is overturning them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The exchange belongs to the story of Aad, but the surah is placing it in front of an audience making the same two moves in the same order. Meccan opponents also treated the message as an attack on inherited worship and repeatedly demanded that the promised punishment be produced on the spot. No specific occasion is reported for the ayah; its force comes from the parallel the surah is drawing.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to overturn or upend something. The same root gives the word this surah uses earlier for a fabrication, so the charge is not error but deliberate inversion.
The possessive is doing the work. What is defended is not a doctrine about the divine but a set of objects belonging to them, tied to their ancestors and their standing.
A plural, which turns the challenge into a question about which company he belongs to. Truthfulness is treated as a class a person is inside or outside, rather than as a quality of one statement.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Gods in that world were also property and history. A tribe's images sat in a known place, had custodians drawn from particular families, and drew visitors whose offerings supported the people around them. Abandoning them meant abandoning an inheritance, an income and a claim to be who your fathers were. That is why the objection is phrased as being turned away from ours rather than as a dispute about what is true.
studies.didYouKnow: The demand phrased here, bring us what you promise us if you are truthful, appears three times in the Quran in almost identical wording. Once it is said to Noah, once to the messenger sent to Aad in another surah, and once here. The Quran presents the dare as a recurring formula rather than as anything the speakers had thought up.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage exposes what a demand for proof can conceal. Asking for the punishment now sets a condition that could only be met by ending the very reprieve the warning exists to offer, so the test is designed to be unpassable while sounding reasonable. It also shows attachment operating before argument. The objection begins with our gods, and everything after that is defence of a possession rather than examination of a claim.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same people the same reply, worded almost identically, in the fuller telling of this episode.
Shows Noah's people making the identical demand after a long argument they had grown tired of.
Records Meccan opponents daring God to rain stones on them if the message were the truth.

studies.applyIt: Listen for the possessive next time you defend a position hard. Our way, my field, the people I came up with. It is often the first word out and the least examined. You do not have to change your mind about anything today. Just notice, once, when you are protecting an inheritance and calling it an argument.

studies.title: The Knowledge Is With God
studies.meaning: The reply refuses the frame instead of meeting the challenge. Asked to produce the punishment, the messenger says the timing is not his to hold, which concedes the one thing his opponents assumed a truthful man would have. He then names his own function with a verb of delivery, the word for making something reach its destination unaltered. The last clause is a judgement, but the verb behind it covers rashness as much as unawareness, so what he sees in them is a way of behaving rather than a gap in their information.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, inside the account of Aad, and shaped so that it answers the Meccan audience at the same time. Opponents in Mecca repeatedly asked when the promised reckoning would come, and the answer given to them elsewhere is the answer given here. The commentators treat this as the standard prophetic reply to a demand for timing, and report no particular occasion behind this ayah.

keyTerms.note: With the definite article and no object named, so it means the knowledge of the matter under discussion. The restriction is placed on him first, before it is turned into a claim about them.
A causative of arriving: to make something reach its destination. It is a courier's word, describing delivery without alteration, and the messenger uses it to define the whole of his role.
The root covers not knowing and behaving rashly at once. In older Arabic it names hot-headedness as much as unawareness, so the charge concerns temperament rather than a lack of facts.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A message in that world moved by human carrier. A man was given words to memorise and repeat exactly, and his standing rested on delivering them without addition, however unwelcome they were at the other end. Chiefs sent such messengers between camps during disputes, and harming one was a serious breach. The audience understood a courier's duty precisely, including that he did not own what he carried and could not adjust it.
studies.didYouKnow: The idea in this reply, that the messenger owes only delivery, becomes a fixed phrase in the Quran. A related noun meaning the conveying appears eleven times, usually to close an argument by saying that nothing beyond delivery was ever the messenger's responsibility. The formula turns up in Meccan and Medinan surahs alike, addressed to very different audiences.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two limits are drawn in one sentence. The messenger does not know the timing, and he does not control the response; between those limits sits the only thing he is answerable for. That protects prophecy from becoming prediction, and it also removes the leverage that a demand for a date would give an opponent. What remains is a claim that can be accepted or refused but not tested on the challenger's schedule.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same answer to the same question: the knowledge is with God, and I am a clear warner.
Answers a demand for the hour of the reckoning by placing that knowledge entirely with God.
States the division plainly: yours is the delivering, and the reckoning belongs to God.

studies.applyIt: Pick the argument you keep losing with someone you love, and work out which part of it is actually yours. Usually it is one sentence, and the rest is trying to control what they do with it. Say your sentence once this week, plainly, and then let the outcome go. That division is what the ayah is describing.

studies.title: A Cloud They Called Rain
studies.meaning: The mistake they make is a reasonable one. A bank of cloud comes in across their valleys, and in that country cloud means water, pasture and another year, so they read it the way their whole experience had trained them to. The correction arrives without any transition: this is the thing you were in a hurry for. The same word for the cloud stands twice in the ayah, once in the narration and once in their mouths, so a single sight is shown carrying two entirely different meanings. What comes is wind.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, inside the account of the people of Aad, told to an audience that had just been told the surah's opponents make the same demands. The dare in the previous ayat was to produce the punishment. This ayah answers it, and the answer arrives disguised as the thing most wanted. The classical commentators report no separate occasion; they read the sequence as a single narrative unit about a challenge and its reply.

keyTerms.gloss: a cloud showing across the sky
keyTerms.note: From a root for presenting something sideways. It names a bank of cloud lying broad along the horizon, and the word appears in the Quran only in this ayah, where it stands twice.
An active participle rather than a hope. Their certainty is built into the grammar: not this might bring rain, but this one is our rain, which is what makes the correction land so hard.
A form meaning to ask that something be brought forward in time. It points back at their own challenge a few ayat earlier, so the arrival is framed as a request being granted.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rain was the single event that organised the year. Whole tribes watched the sky in the seasons when it might come, and the sighting of cloud over the wadis was news that travelled between camps within a day. After a good fall, dry watercourses ran, grazing appeared in places that had been bare for months, and herds were moved to meet it. Nothing in that world was better news than a cloud in the right direction.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran describes the end of Aad several times and gives the wind a different description each time: a screaming wind, a devastating wind, a furious roaring one that continued for seven nights and eight days. This ayah is the only one that shows the moment before it, when the thing on the horizon was still being read as good news.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage says something uncomfortable about signs. The cloud is a real sign and it is read with ordinary competence, and the reading is wrong, because the meaning of an event is not fully contained in its appearance. That does not make observation useless. It sets a limit on it, and the limit is exactly where the previous ayat placed knowledge, with God. The same shape arrives as mercy elsewhere in the Quran and as its opposite here.

crossReferences.why: Shows the same sequence, wind then heavy cloud then water, running the other way, as mercy.
Describes the wind sent against Aad, sparing nothing it came upon and leaving it like decayed ruins.
Gives the duration, seven nights and eight days, and asks whether any remnant of them can be seen.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you are currently certain is good news arriving. A job offer, a move, a person. Do not talk yourself out of it. Just hold it a little more loosely for a day, the way you would hold a forecast rather than a fact. The people in this ayah were not foolish. They were confident, and their confidence was the last thing they had.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Nothing Left But The Houses
studies.meaning: The destruction is total and it is placed under an order. The wind wrecks everything by its Lord's command, which names the authority behind the weather without softening the weather itself. Then comes morning, and one thing is still standing: their dwellings. The commentators read this as the houses being left deliberately, as evidence. The people are gone and the architecture survives them, which reverses the ordinary picture of ruin, where buildings fall and populations move on. The closing sentence uses an ongoing tense, so a single night becomes a description of a pattern.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Ruined sites were part of the landscape Arabian traders moved through, and the Quran refers to them repeatedly as things its audience could go and look at. The commentators place Aad in the sandy south of the peninsula and note that this ayah supplies the moment of the ending rather than the cause. No specific occasion is reported for it; it completes the narrative begun several ayat earlier.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form of a verb for ruining beyond repair. The subject is the wind and the authority is named in the same breath, so the destruction is described as carried out under instruction.
From the root for stillness and settling, since a dwelling is where movement stops. The word appears twice in the Quran in this form, and both times it names what is left after the people have gone.
A verb from the language of wages and returned favours. Its tense here is the continuous one, which turns the single event just described into a statement about how things work.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Empty settlements were ordinary sights on the trade roads. Wells silted up, an irrigation channel failed, a route shifted, and a town emptied within a generation while its walls stayed standing for centuries. Caravans camped in such places, and the stories attached to them were part of what a young man learned on his first journey north or south. An audience that had slept inside abandoned houses did not need this image explained.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for their dwellings occurs in only one other place in the Quran, in a passage about towns destroyed for ingratitude toward their own livelihood. There too the point is that the buildings remain visible and unoccupied. In both, the surviving architecture is treated as the evidence rather than the loss.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage insists on an agent behind an event that looks like weather, and it does so with a single phrase rather than an argument. That matters because natural causes and divine command are not offered here as alternatives; the wind does its own work, and the instruction is named alongside it. The shift to a continuous tense at the end has a similar effect. A story about one people becomes a claim about a standing order rather than a memory.

crossReferences.why: Contains the same word for dwellings left standing and unoccupied after a town was destroyed.
Points the audience at the ruins of Aad and Thamud as something already clear to them.
Shows the houses of another destroyed people preserved as a sign for those who understand.

studies.applyIt: If you pass an empty building this week, a closed shop or a boarded house, give it ten seconds. Somebody chose the paint. The ayah works on exactly that gap between how long a thing lasts and how long the person who made it lasts, and the gap is easier to feel in front of a real doorway than in an argument.

studies.title: Hearing, Sight And Hearts
studies.meaning: The comparison is aimed straight at the listener: they were given a firmer footing than you have. Then three faculties are listed, and the same three are repeated in the same order to say that not one of them helped. The repetition is the argument. Equipment is not the problem, and neither is information. The reason given is a verb that means denying what you actually recognise, which is a decision rather than a defect. The last clause closes the circle: the thing they had been laughing at came round and settled over them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and pointed. Mecca's confidence rested on its trade, its sanctuary and its standing among the tribes, and the ayah measures that confidence against a people the Arabs remembered as far more powerful. The commentators note the direct address, since the ayah stops narrating and speaks to the audience in the middle of the sentence. No occasion is reported; the force is in the comparison itself.

keyTerms.note: A plural of a word for the heart taken as the organ of comprehension, distinct from the more common term. Its pairing with hearing and sight forms the Quran's standard inventory of what a person is given.

Arabic reserves this verb for refusal against recognition, as when a man denies a debt he clearly remembers owing. It is not a word for ignorance, which is why the faculties listed made no difference.
To surround and settle upon from every side. The Quran uses it almost exclusively of a consequence coming back to the people who set it going, which is why mockery is its subject here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Aad were the standard Arabian example of strength that did not last. Poets used them for the way a modern speaker uses a fallen empire, and southern Arabia held the physical evidence: dams, terraced hillsides and stone towers built by people who had commanded labour on a scale Mecca could not. A Meccan merchant with two hundred camels heard this comparison as a downgrade, which is precisely how the ayah frames it.
studies.didYouKnow: The triad of hearing, sight and hearts appears in several places in the Quran, and in the other passages it is nearly always followed by a note that people give little thanks for them. Here the same three are listed and followed instead by the statement that they availed nothing, which turns a familiar sentence about gratitude into one about failure.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates capacity from use, and it puts the whole weight on the second. Faculties are described as given, which makes them gifts rather than achievements, and then shown to be inert when the will has already decided. That protects the Quran's constant appeals to look and to listen from becoming naive, since the same appeals are made to people it says will not be moved by them. What fails here is not the eye. It is the recognition the eye delivered.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same three faculties as things provided at birth, so that a person might be thankful.
Repeats the list and adds that rarely do people give thanks for any of them.
Locates the real blindness in the hearts inside the chests rather than in the eyes.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing today you already know and have arranged not to look at. A bill, a scan result, a conversation you keep postponing. The ayah is not about people who lacked eyes. Look at the one thing, for as long as it takes to read it properly, and notice how much of the difficulty was never about not knowing.

studies.title: Why Did They Not Help
studies.meaning: Two ayat, two different kinds of pressure. The first is geographical: ruined settlements lie around you, and the signs were turned about in many forms so that people might come back. The second is a question with an edge on it. Those they had adopted as a way of drawing nearer to God, why did they not come? The answer given is not that they were powerless but that they went missing, which is worse. The last clause names the whole arrangement, and it uses the word for something turned upside down.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ruined places the ayah points at were known ones: Thamud's carved dwellings on the northern trade route, the country associated with Aad to the south, and settlements on the Syrian road remembered for their destruction. Meccan caravans passed them twice a year. The commentators identify the intermediaries described here as the practice of approaching God through lesser powers rather than as outright denial of God, which the Quran addresses elsewhere.

keyTerms.note: An offering made to close a distance. Its only other occurrence in this form describes the sacrifice brought by Adam's two sons, so the word carries the sense of something given up to gain access.
To turn a thing this way and that, as the wind is turned. Applied to signs it means presenting the same point from many angles, which describes a method rather than a single message.
The verb for wandering off the path, used here of the objects rather than of the worshippers. The accusation usually aimed at people is turned on what they trusted, at the moment of need.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Protection in Mecca was a named relationship. A man under the protection of a strong clan could trade and travel; without it he was exposed, and the whole city knew which arrangement covered whom. Such protection could also be publicly withdrawn, and when it was, the man was ruined within a day. Asking why the protectors did not come is not an abstract question in that setting. It is the question everyone feared having to ask.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran elsewhere quotes the reasoning behind the practice described here almost word for word, where people say they worship these only so that they may bring them nearer to God. That makes the arrangement an intermediary one rather than a rival religion, and it is why the question in this ayah is about help arriving rather than about existence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage tests a religious arrangement by asking what it does when everything else fails.
