That is a hard standard and a fair one, since the intermediaries had been adopted precisely for access and support. It also describes revelation's method in a single word: the same signs turned about, presented from different angles, aimed at return rather than at defeat. The purpose clause matters. Destruction is reported, but what is said to be intended is people coming back.

crossReferences.why: Quotes the rationale directly: we worship them only so they may bring us nearer to God.
Calls the same intermediaries intercessors with God, and asks whether God is being informed of something.
Uses the same verb for turning the signs about, in a passage about how they are presented.

studies.applyIt: Make a short list of what you rely on when things go badly. Not what you say you rely on. Savings, a particular friend, your own competence, a substance, a screen. Nothing on that list has to be removed. Just notice which items have already failed once, and whether you put them back on the list anyway.

studies.title: A Small Band Came Listening
studies.meaning: The scene is told with unusual economy. A group is turned toward the recitation, arrives while it is under way, and the first thing they say is a single word to each other: be quiet and listen. When it finishes they leave at once and go back to their own people carrying a warning. Nothing is reported about what convinced them, what they understood, or how long they stayed. The entire episode is compressed into hearing and then going home, which is itself the point being made.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The classical sources connect this to a night on the return from Ta'if, when the recitation was heard on the road, and they report the details differently from one another. What they broadly agree on is the setting: a period when the human audience in Mecca had largely closed, the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) had been rejected in a second town, and the surah records a hearing that came from an unexpected direction.

keyTerms.note: A group small enough to be counted, and one that has set out for something rather than gathered by chance. The word implies a party on an errand, which fits a group described as having been directed there.

One verb covering both halves of listening, stopping your own noise and turning toward the sound. It occurs twice in the Quran, the other time describing what is asked of anyone present at a recitation.
The plural of the word the surah has been using for messengers. Here it lands on the listeners themselves, so the role passes to people who have heard the recitation once and are on their way home.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Recitation happened aloud and at night. Travellers slept in the open near the road, and a voice carrying in still desert air reaches much further than people expect. Meccan opponents were sufficiently worried about this that they discouraged visitors from stopping to listen, and some are reported to have crept out to hear at night and hidden the fact from each other. Hearing at a distance, unannounced and unwelcomed, was how the recitation actually spread.
studies.didYouKnow: The word the group uses on arriving, telling each other to fall silent and listen, occurs only twice in the whole Quran. Its other appearance is in a general instruction about how the recitation is to be received. Here that same instruction is not given to anyone; it is what the listeners say to each other without being told.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage widens the audience of revelation beyond the human race, and it does so almost casually, without argument or defence. It also gives a compact picture of how a message is received: attention first, then transmission, with no interval for deliberation described. Set against the surah's long record of people who heard clearly and refused, the contrast is not about evidence. Both groups received the same recitation. Only one of them stopped talking.

crossReferences.why: Gives the jinn's own account of the same kind of hearing, in their words rather than in narration.
Contains the other occurrence of the word they use, in a general instruction about receiving recitation.
Reports what followed for them: hearing the guidance, believing, and fearing neither loss nor burden.

studies.applyIt: Listen to a short recitation today without doing anything else. Not in the car, not while cooking. The instruction this group gave each other was about noise, theirs and everyone's. Three minutes with nothing else running is a fair test of whether you have ever actually done what they did, or only had it playing.

studies.title: A Book After Moses
studies.meaning: What they report is a summary with a definite shape: a scripture, its place in a sequence, its relation to what came before, and the direction it points. The article is indefinite. They say a book, not the book, which is what a first encounter sounds like from inside. The striking detail is the name they use to date it. They place it after Moses rather than after anyone later, and the commentators note this and offer several readings, some tying the group to knowledge of the Torah, others taking Moses as the marker for scripture given as law.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the closing section of a surah that has spent most of its length recording refusals. The classical sources place the episode on a journey when the recitation was heard by night, and the reports differ over the location and the number involved. What the ayah supplies is the content of what was carried away, which the other account of this hearing, in a later surah, gives in different words.

keyTerms.note: The address every messenger in the Quran uses toward his own community, with the possessive attached. Here it is spoken by listeners returning home rather than by anyone who was sent.
Indefinite. They are reporting an encounter rather than making a claim about rank, and the grammar keeps the sentence at the level of what they actually heard rather than what it is.
This exact pairing occurs once in the Quran. It uses the ordinary word for a track or route rather than the more familiar term for a broad paved way, which is used everywhere else.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: News travelled by the person who happened to be there. A man came back from a market or a season away, and what he had seen became his people's account of it, repeated in his words for years. Accuracy mattered and was checked, since a traveller who exaggerated lost his standing. What this group does is entirely ordinary in that world: they were present at something, and they went home and gave the report.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for a straight road used at the end of this ayah appears in this exact form only here. The Quran's usual expression for the same idea uses a different noun, one that suggests a broad paved way, and it occurs more than twenty times. The variation sits inside a speech that is being quoted from speakers who are not human.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The summary given here is a small piece of theology in its own right. A revelation is identified by continuity rather than by novelty, and its authority is described through what it confirms and where it leads rather than through the power of the one who brought it. The dating from Moses says something similar. Scripture is presented as a line with places on it, so recognising a new arrival means locating it, not being overwhelmed by it.

crossReferences.why: Gives the other report of this hearing, describing a wondrous recitation that guides to rectitude.
Uses the same description of the Book as confirming what came before it, alongside the earlier scriptures.
Sets out the relation at length: revealed with truth, confirming what preceded it, and standing as a guardian over it.

studies.applyIt: Try describing what you believe to someone in four clauses, the way this group did. What it is, where it came from, what it agrees with, where it leads. No defence, no argument. Most people find they have never assembled the sentence, and the difficulty of writing it down is more useful than any answer you would have given.

studies.title: Answer The One Who Calls
studies.meaning: The appeal has a clean structure: two things asked, two things offered. Answer the caller and believe, and forgiveness and rescue follow. The grammar of the forgiveness clause has occupied commentators, since the preposition before sins is the one that ordinarily means some of, and they explain it in several ways without agreeing. The second promise uses the vocabulary of shelter. It is the verb for taking someone under formal protection when he is being hunted, which makes the offer sound less like a pardon and more like a granted asylum.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This is the second half of a report brought home by listeners who had heard the recitation once, and it comes near the end of a surah otherwise filled with refusals. Protection was a live institution in Mecca at the time: the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) had himself returned to the city under the formal protection of a man outside his own clan after being turned away elsewhere.

keyTerms.note: The word for a man summoning people to a gathering or to a meal, not a title of office. This phrase occurs twice in the Quran, here and in the ayah immediately following it.
The formal act by which a clan sheltered someone from those pursuing him. The verb carries an obligation to defend, which is a good deal more than wishing a person well.
From a root connected with the tail of an animal, the part that trails behind. A wrong in this vocabulary is a thing with consequences following it, which is what the second promise addresses.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Asylum was a public and binding arrangement. A man in danger sought a protector, and if the protector accepted, he announced it, and an attack on the protected man became an attack on the whole clan. It could be granted to a stranger, and it held even when the protector disliked the man's cause. Honour depended on keeping it. To that audience, the second promise here is a legal form they had watched being performed.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact clause promising forgiveness of your sins occurs twice in the Quran. Once it is here, spoken by a group of jinn urging their own people to accept what they had heard. The other time it is Noah, appealing to his people over a much longer span of years. Both times the words are in the mouth of a speaker addressing his own community.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The offer is made by listeners rather than by a messenger, which quietly widens who is entitled to make it. Beyond that, the pairing of the two promises is precise. Forgiveness deals with the record and protection deals with what follows the record, and the passage does not merge them into a single vague reassurance. The condition attached is also unusually light: answer, and believe. Nothing about status, lineage, or a history clean enough to qualify.

crossReferences.why: Contains the same clause about forgiveness of sins, in Noah's long appeal to his own people.
Describes the Prophet's role in the same terms, as one who calls toward God by His leave.
Turns the direction around: God answers the call of the one who calls on Him.

studies.applyIt: Notice who invited you into something good and never got thanked for it. A teacher, a cousin, whoever first put a book in your hand. The people speaking here had heard one recitation and immediately went to fetch their own community. Send that person a message today. Say only what they did, and that you remember it.

studies.title: Nowhere On Earth To Go
studies.meaning: This is the other half of the invitation just made, and the pairing is deliberate. The first ayah offered forgiveness and shelter; this one removes the two things a person might rely on instead. He cannot put himself beyond reach on the earth, and there is no set of allies standing behind him. The word for allies is the strong one, used of clans in a standing alliance rather than of friends, and the sentence gives it nothing to attach to. The verdict at the end is short and uses the vocabulary of losing a road.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, spoken by a group of listeners to their own people rather than by a messenger, which is unusual for a warning of this kind. It closes the report they carried home after hearing the recitation once. The surah has by this point recorded several refusals and one acceptance, and it lets the accepting party state both sides of the choice in their own words before the surah turns to its final instruction.

keyTerms.note: An active participle from a verb meaning to render someone unable. It describes not merely getting away but leaving the pursuer powerless, and the word occurs in the Quran only here in this form.
The word for parties bound in mutual support, used of clans in a standing alliance. It is stronger than friendship, and the ayah names the category only to say the space behind it is empty.
The state of having lost the track, not of having chosen a bad one. Arabic uses the same word for a man wandering in country he does not know and for a thing that has gone missing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Escape in that world meant distance and a sponsor. A man in trouble could ride out to another tribe and ask to be taken in, and whole feuds were settled by someone crossing the desert to a relative by marriage. Everybody knew the map of who would take whom. The two things this ayah denies are precisely the two moves a person in danger would have made: run far enough, or find the right door.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase closing this ayah, being in obvious error, is one of the Quran's set expressions and appears eighteen times, in the mouths of very different speakers. It is said by opponents about believers and by believers about opponents, and once by Joseph's brothers about their own father. The same words carry the judgement in every direction.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The two ayat together set out a structure the Quran keeps returning to: an offer and a consequence, given in the same breath and by the same speaker. Neither is presented as more real than the other. What this half adds is a claim about scale, since escape and protection both depend on there being somewhere outside the situation to stand. The passage says there is no outside, and it says it in geographical language rather than metaphysical.

crossReferences.why: Has the jinn reach the same conclusion in their own account: they cannot escape God on earth or by fleeing.
States the same denial for the whole creation, on earth and in heaven, with no protector or helper.
Describes the guardians that do surround a person, and where their protection ultimately comes from.

studies.applyIt: Think about your own version of the second door in this ayah, the person or arrangement you assume would catch you. Do not stop trusting it. Just name it accurately, out loud, once. Most of us keep a vague sense that something would hold, and the vagueness is what the ayah is removing, not the trust.

studies.title: And Was Not Wearied
studies.meaning: The argument moves from something granted to something denied, and the hinge is a clause about tiredness. Creating the heavens and the earth is not disputed by the audience. What the ayah inserts is that the making cost nothing, and from there the conclusion follows: a maker who was not depleted by the larger work is not short of what the smaller one needs. The answer comes back in a single particle of emphatic assent, and then a general statement replaces the specific one. The word for weariness here occurs nowhere else in the Quran.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Denial of bodily resurrection was the sharpest point of disagreement, and the objection was usually put as a practical impossibility rather than as a theological claim: scattered bones cannot be gathered. The Quran answers that objection repeatedly, and almost always by pointing at something the objector already accepts. No specific occasion is reported here. The ayah closes the surah's long argument before its final instruction.

keyTerms.gloss: grew weary, was at a loss
keyTerms.note: A verb covering both physical exhaustion and being unable to find a way forward. It appears only in this ayah in the whole Quran, which puts unusual weight on a very ordinary word.
A particle that contradicts a negative question rather than merely agreeing with it. It cannot be used to say yes to an ordinary question, so its presence marks the doubt as already assumed.
An intensive form from a root that also gives the words for measure and decree. Ability in this vocabulary includes proportioning, so it is capacity that knows the exact amount required.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything in that world was made by hand and everyone knew what making cost. A well took weeks and left men ruined; a wall was built by people who then rested; a long weaving was measured in days out of a woman's life. Effort was visible in the object. That is precisely the intuition the ayah interrupts, because an audience that assumed a great work must exhaust its maker would conclude that a later, smaller work might be beyond him.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for weariness in this ayah occurs nowhere else in the Quran. A closely related idea appears four surahs later, where the six days of creation are said to have been completed without any fatigue touching God, using a different word that also occurs only once. Both statements arrive in the same argument about raising the dead.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage argues from creation to resurrection by way of a denial about God rather than a claim about power. That is a subtle move, because it removes the analogy people naturally bring, in which large tasks drain a maker and small ones are easy afterward. It also shows the Quran's habitual method: begin where the audience already stands, add one thing they had not considered, and let the conclusion arrive without being insisted on.

crossReferences.why: Denies fatigue after the six days of creation, in the same kind of argument about raising the dead.
Puts the identical question the other way: is the maker of the heavens not able to make their like.
Traces a human being back to a drop and ends by asking whether that maker cannot revive the dead.

studies.applyIt: Think of the largest thing you have ever finished, and how long it took you to feel normal afterward. Then notice how automatically you carry that experience into what you expect of God. The ayah is aimed at exactly that transfer. You do not need to argue with it. Just catch yourself doing it once today.

studies.title: Presented A Second Time
studies.meaning: This ayah opens with the same clause that opened one fourteen ayat earlier, word for word, so the surah shows the same scene twice with different content. The first time the charge concerned a life spent entirely on itself. Here nothing is charged at all. A question is asked about whether this is real, and the answer is an emphatic yes reinforced by an oath. The verb for being presented is the one used for inspecting ranks or displaying goods before a buyer, which makes the moment an examination rather than a punishment.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has been arguing about resurrection for its whole length, and this is where the argument stops being an argument. The commentators note the repetition of the opening clause and treat the pair as bracketing the section on Aad and the jinn between them. No specific occasion is reported. The ayah's force in Mecca lay in describing the opponents' own future words rather than answering their present ones.

keyTerms.note: The verb for showing something for inspection, used of ranks of soldiers passing before a commander and of goods laid out for a buyer. It makes the scene an examination rather than an act of force.
The particle that answers a negative question by overturning it. Answering with it means conceding the very thing the question assumed they would deny, which is why no argument follows.
A verb of direct sensation rather than of enduring. Tasting is the most immediate kind of knowledge, and the word is chosen against a lifetime of treating the matter as something argued about.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An oath by God was the most serious speech available to an Arab. It closed disputes that no evidence could settle, and a man who swore falsely was understood to have staked something he could not recover. The heaviest oaths were reserved for matters of blood and property. The people in this scene use that formula, and they use it to confirm a thing they had spent their lives declining to say in ordinary speech.
studies.didYouKnow: The same exchange appears almost word for word in an earlier surah, where a group stationed before their Lord is asked whether this is not the truth and answers with the identical oath. The two passages differ by only a few words. The Quran shows the same moment twice, in different chapters, using the same short script.
studies.theologicalSignificance: What is missing from this scene is any dispute. Nobody argues, nobody pleads ignorance, and nobody is shown being convinced by evidence. That has a specific implication: the passage does not treat the last day as the moment when the truth is established, but as the moment when it becomes impossible to hold anything else. The difference between the two lives the surah has described is therefore located entirely in the present, where holding something else is still possible.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same exchange in almost identical words, including the oath and the reply that follows.
Opens with the identical clause fourteen ayat earlier, and brings a very different charge with it.
Describes the same presentation before the Fire, there as something happening morning and evening.

studies.applyIt: Pick a thing you already know is true and have not said out loud, about your health, your work, or someone you love. Say it once today to one person, in plain words. The scene in this ayah is not about discovering anything. It is about the delay between knowing and admitting, and that delay is entirely yours to shorten.

studies.title: As The Resolute Ones Were
studies.meaning: The surah's closing instruction is a comparison rather than a command in the abstract: be patient in the way particular earlier messengers were. The commentators differ over who is meant, some taking it as all the messengers and most naming a small group distinguished by long endurance, and the phrase itself occurs only here. A second instruction follows, not to seek to hasten things for the opponents, which turns impatience into a request. Then the reason: on the day they see what was promised, the whole span behind them will feel like an hour of daylight.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, at the end of a surah that has recorded refusal after refusal and one unexpected acceptance. The instruction addresses a situation of prolonged rejection rather than of danger, which is why patience is the last word rather than rescue. The commentators connect the second clause to the demands for immediate punishment quoted earlier in the same surah, and read it as forbidding the messenger the impatience his opponents had shown.

keyTerms.note: A phrase occurring once in the Quran. The noun means a settled determination reached after deliberation, not a burst of will, and the commentators differ on whether it names all messengers or a few.
The same verb the opponents used earlier in this surah when they dared the punishment to arrive. Placing it here turns their taunt into a temptation, and the messenger is told to refuse it.
A single word standing alone as a sentence: this is a conveyance. It names the whole surah as something handed over, and it appears in this bare form only twice in the Quran.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Time was reckoned by daylight and by the tasks that filled it. An hour of a day was not a measured unit but the space of a task, the time to water a herd or reach the next well. Long journeys were remembered in stages rather than in numbers, and travellers routinely arrived surprised at how short the crossing had felt in retrospect. The comparison at the end of the ayah uses the audience's own way of measuring.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase describing messengers of firm resolve occurs only in this ayah, and the Quran never lists who they are. Classical commentators supply the names from other passages where prophets are grouped together, most often taking the five who are named side by side in two places as the intended group, while others hold that the phrase covers all the messengers.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Patience is defined here by imitation rather than by definition, which locates it in a history rather than in a virtue list. The second half then supplies its ground. Duration is real while it is being lived and negligible from the far side, and the passage does not deny the first half of that in order to assert the second. Waiting is treated as genuinely long. What changes is the vantage point from which its length will eventually be judged.

crossReferences.why: Names five messengers together in a covenant, the group most often identified with this phrase.
Uses the same measure, describing them gathered as though they had tarried an hour of a day.
Gives the same instruction, a beautiful patience, alongside the reason that the distant looks near.

studies.applyIt: Choose one thing you have been waiting on and stop checking it for a week. A message, a result, a decision someone else is making. Checking is the small form of asking for it to be brought forward. You are not being asked to feel calm about it. Only to stop reaching for the outcome with your hands.
